threads.thread_goal: Align on current process, main gaps, and project scope before design work starts.

messages.text:
Kicking off the Cross-Department Protocol for High-Risk Detainee Health Monitoring project.

Goal: agree what parts of the prison and which detainees this protocol will cover, and confirm the current process map as our baseline.

I have pulled together a draft of the current detainee health monitoring and incident escalation process for T1, which is reflected in the process map in A1. It covers intake, routine checks, and incident escalation as I understand them from existing notes and a quick chat with one unit supervisor.

Two questions for everyone:
1) Scope: should we focus first on one unit or all units, and are we limiting this to detainees flagged as high-risk, or everyone with a health note?
2) Gaps: from your day-to-day experience, what is missing or inaccurate in the flow shown in A1 so we can finalise T1?

@504576 I would really value your view from the floor. @19315 can you check if anything in A1 conflicts with current admin routines?

Thanks for sharing the draft.

On scope: from an operational point of view, I suggest we start with one residential unit plus the intake area. Most of the health-related issues we see either start at intake or during the first week on the wing. If we try to cover the whole prison at once, it will be hard to keep it consistent.

On detainees: I would not limit the protocol only to those already flagged as high-risk. We often only realise someone is at risk after a few minor incidents. I would prefer a light-touch protocol that applies to all detainees, with clearer escalation steps once certain signs are present.

On A1: the intake part looks close to what we do, but I do not see the informal checks we do during meal distribution and evening lock-up. Those are often when we notice changes in behaviour. Also, the handover to night staff is a bit simplified; there is usually a quick verbal briefing as well as the written log.

I have reviewed A1 against our current admin routines.

From the admin side, the main steps are captured, but a few details are missing:
- When a health concern is logged, admin staff usually create a paper note for the medical team and file a copy in the detainee folder. That is not clearly shown.
- For incident escalation, there is a separate incident form that goes to management and sometimes to legal, depending on severity. That branch is not visible in the current map.

For T1, I can add these steps and mark where admin staff receive information from officers and where we send it on to medical or management. I will also check with one of the managers to confirm the escalation path for serious incidents so A1 reflects the formal route, not just the informal practice.

From the health perspective, I agree with focusing on intake plus one residential unit first. That will give us enough variation in cases without overcomplicating the first version.

On detainee scope, I support applying the monitoring steps to everyone, with a clearer flag once certain signs are present. That will also make it easier later when we define indicators for T2.

Looking at A1, I notice that there is no explicit step where someone reviews patterns over time, for example repeated minor complaints or changes in behaviour. Everything seems event-based. For the protocol, it would help if we add a point where either an officer or admin reviews the log at least once per shift or per day to spot trends. That will also connect better with the central log we plan in T5.

This is helpful, thanks.

On scope, I hear: intake area plus one residential unit, and a protocol that technically applies to all detainees but has clearer steps once certain signs are present.

Before we lock that in, any objections to that approach from an admin or design point of view? It will influence how we frame T1 and the later SOP in T3.

From the forms and layout side, starting with intake plus one unit sounds manageable. If we tried to cover all areas at once, we might end up with too many variations of the checklist.

For me, it would help if A1 clearly shows where officers are already filling in any paper forms, so that when I work on the checklists for T4 I can see whether we are adding a new sheet or adjusting an existing one.

No objection from my side. Intake plus one residential unit is also easier to coordinate for scheduling and filing.

For T1, I will update A1 to:
- Add the informal checks during meals and evening lock-up that @504576 mentioned.
- Show the admin steps for creating notes for medical and filing copies.
- Add the branch for serious incident forms going to management and, where relevant, legal.
- Insert a daily or per-shift review step, as suggested by @6456, so we have a clear point where someone looks at patterns.

Once I have that version, I will validate it with one officer and one manager as required for T1.

Happy to be the officer who validates the updated A1 for T1.

One more gap I noticed: when we call medical for an urgent check, there is sometimes a delay before they arrive. During that time, we usually increase observation and sometimes move the detainee closer to the office. That interim step is not shown but is important for risk.

Could we add a box for that interim observation period, including who is responsible for watching the detainee and what should be recorded?

That interim period is critical from a health point of view. If we add it into A1, we can later tie it to specific observation points when we work on T2.

I suggest we define, at least at a high level in the process map, that during this period officers:
- Keep the detainee within direct line of sight.
- Note any changes in breathing, level of consciousness, or agitation.
- Record the time of any change.

We can keep the details light in A1 and expand them in the indicators guide later.

Good point. I will add an explicit interim observation step into A1, with a note that the unit officer in charge is responsible for monitoring and recording changes until medical arrives.

For T1, I will also list this interim period as one of the current pain points, since we do not have a standard way of documenting it yet.

Thanks all. To move us forward, I propose we formalise the scope so we can close T1 and move on to the design work.

Proposal:
- Units: intake area plus one residential unit (to be named in the pilot plan later).
- Detainees: protocol steps apply to all detainees in those areas, with additional escalation once certain signs are present.

If no one objects by tomorrow, I will record this as our agreed scope for the protocol.
I am comfortable with that scope. It matches how we work and should be realistic for a first implementation.
No objections from admin. I will reflect that scope in the updated A1 and in the notes for T1.

Great, then we will proceed with that scope.

On the current-state map: once @19315 has incorporated the changes discussed and you, @504576, and one manager have validated it, I suggest we treat A1 as our baseline for design.

Please confirm once that validation is done so we can formally adopt A1 as the reference for the next tasks.

Update: I have now revised A1 with all the points raised and walked through it with @504576 and the unit manager.

They confirmed that the steps for intake, routine checks, interim observation while waiting for medical, and escalation paths match current practice, with the admin branches added.

Unless anyone spots a major issue, I suggest we confirm A1 as the baseline for the design work linked to T3, T4, and T5.
From my side, the updated A1 is sufficient as a baseline. It captures the key points where health-related information appears and where we can later attach indicators and checklists.

I confirm that the latest A1 reflects what we actually do on the unit, including the informal checks and the interim observation period. I am fine with using it as the starting point for the new protocol.

Thanks everyone. To summarise this thread:
- Scope: intake area plus one residential unit; protocol applies to all detainees there, with clearer escalation once certain signs are present.
- Baseline: the validated version of A1 is now our agreed current-state map and will guide the SOP (T3), checklists (T4), and log template (T5).

Next, we can move into defining the health indicators and observation points, and then translate those into practical forms and procedures.

threads.thread_goal: Define practical health risk indicators and observation checklists for officers.

messages.text:
Following our agreed scope and baseline in A1, I am sharing a draft set of health risk indicators for T2 and a first outline for the observation checklist that will become A3.

For A2, I have grouped indicators into three categories:
- Physical signs: breathing difficulty, chest pain, severe headache, visible injuries, signs of intoxication or withdrawal.
- Behavioural signs: sudden withdrawal, agitation, confusion, talking about self-harm, not responding when spoken to.
- Contextual factors: recent use of force, recent arrival, known chronic conditions, recent bad news.

For each, I have tried to use plain language and added a simple rule of thumb for when to escalate.

For A3, the idea is a one-page checklist for intake and a shorter version for routine patrols, both aligned with A2.

@504576 could you comment on whether this feels usable during a busy shift? @444619 I would like your view on how to lay this out on paper for T4 so it is quick to scan.

The categories make sense and match what we see on the unit.

A few practical points:
- On physical signs, it would help to distinguish between things that require immediate call to medical or emergency services and things that can wait until the next round.
- Behavioural signs: we often see low-level agitation or mood changes. If we mark everything, the checklist might become too heavy. Maybe we can highlight a few combinations that are more worrying.
- Contextual factors: recent use of force and recent arrival are easy to track. Known chronic conditions are sometimes not clearly communicated to us, so we should not rely on that alone.

On A3 length: during patrols, we have very little time. A short list with tick boxes and maybe a free-text line for anything unusual would be best. Intake can handle a bit more detail, but still needs to be quick.

On the layout for T4 and A3, I would suggest:
- For intake: one side of an A4 sheet, grouped by the three categories you listed, with simple tick boxes and a small notes area at the bottom.
- For patrols: a slimmer strip or half-page that can be attached to the existing patrol sheet, with only the most critical items.

I will need to know how many items you want in each category so I can make sure the font is readable and there is enough space for ticks and short notes.

From an admin and documentation angle, it would be useful if A3 clearly indicates where officers should write the detainee ID and date/time, so that when we file these with the central log in A4 later, we can match them easily.

Also, for T2, could we add a simple legend or colour code in A2 that matches the escalation levels we will define in the SOP for T3? That will help keep things consistent.

Thanks for the feedback.

On physical signs, I can split them into two levels in A2:
- Immediate: severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, loss of consciousness, heavy bleeding.
- Urgent but not immediate: moderate pain, mild breathing issues, visible but not severe injuries.

For behavioural signs, I will focus on a smaller set that is strongly linked to risk, such as talking about self-harm, not responding, or sudden extreme agitation, and note that minor mood changes alone do not trigger escalation.

On contextual factors, I will treat known chronic conditions as an extra flag when available, not a requirement.

For A3, I will aim for around 10 items for intake and 6 for patrols, grouped by category, and keep one free-text line for anything unusual.

Good point on consistency.

I will add a simple three-level scale in A2 that we can later align with the SOP in A5 and T3:
- Level 1: note and monitor.
- Level 2: inform supervisor and consider medical review.
- Level 3: immediate emergency response.

For A3, I will include clear fields for detainee ID, date, time, and officer name at the top, so that admin can link them to the central log A4.

If we are aiming for about 10 items on the intake checklist and 6 on the patrol version, I can draft a layout for T4 where each item has a short phrase and a tick box.

For the three-level scale, we could use a small legend at the bottom of A3, matching the wording in A2, so officers do not have to remember what each level means.

The split between immediate and urgent-but-not-immediate sounds workable.

On the patrol checklist, 6 items is probably the upper limit. If we can keep the wording short and clear, officers should be able to scan it quickly during rounds.

One suggestion: could we include an item that reminds us to check for changes compared to the previous shift, not just what we see in the moment? That would support the pattern review you mentioned earlier.

Yes, that is a good addition.

I will add one patrol item along the lines of: noticeable change since last shift in behaviour, appearance, or complaints. That will encourage officers to think about trends, not just single events.

With that, the patrol checklist would have:
- 3 physical items.
- 2 behavioural items.
- 1 change-since-last-shift item.

Does that feel balanced enough for daily use?
Yes, that balance looks right to me. It keeps the focus on the most important points without overloading the patrols.

From the documentation side, the three-level scale and the ID/date/time fields will make it much easier to integrate A3 with the central log A4 and the SOP A5.

Once you finalise the wording in A2, I can check that the terms match what we plan to use in the SOP for T3 so we avoid confusion later.

Great. I will now clean up the draft of A2 with:
- The three categories of indicators.
- The split between immediate and urgent physical signs.
- A focused list of behavioural signs.
- Contextual factors as additional flags.
- The three-level escalation scale.

I will also update the A3 draft to reflect the 10 intake items and 6 patrol items, with the change-since-last-shift item included.

Once that is done, I would like a final confirmation from you, @504576, that the list in A2 is workable for officers, so we can treat it as the agreed set of indicators for the project.

I have reviewed the updated A2 and A3 drafts you sent.

The indicators in A2 are clear and match what we can realistically observe. The three-level scale is understandable, and the examples help.

The intake and patrol versions of A3 are both short enough to use in practice. I am comfortable saying that this list of indicators can be our reference for the protocol.

With the content of A2 and A3 now stable, I will proceed to finalise the layout for T4.

For the structure and length of A3, we are aligned on:
- One-page intake checklist with around 10 items.
- Half-page patrol checklist with 6 items.
- Clear ID/date/time fields and a small notes area.

Unless anyone disagrees, I will treat this as the agreed structure for A3.

From a coordination point of view, that structure for A3 works well and fits within the time constraints we discussed.

I suggest we record that as our agreed checklist structure so that T4 can move ahead without further changes to length or format.

To close this thread, here is a quick summary:
- A2 now contains the agreed list of health risk indicators, grouped into physical, behavioural, and contextual, with a three-level escalation scale and clear examples.
- A3 will consist of a one-page intake checklist and a shorter patrol checklist, with around 10 and 6 items respectively, plus ID/date/time fields and a notes area.

We will use these as the basis for the SOP in A5 and the training materials in T6.

threads.thread_goal: Lock down the SOP, logging template, and filing workflow.

messages.text:
I am sharing the draft SOP for health risk assessment and escalation (A5) and the first version of the central health monitoring log template (A4), both linked to T3 and T5.

Key points in A5:
- Roles: unit officer, supervisor, admin staff, and medical team.
- Steps: observe using A3, classify using A2, record in A4, escalate according to the three-level scale, and document outcomes.
- Escalation paths: Level 1 monitor, Level 2 supervisor and medical review, Level 3 emergency response and incident form.

For A4, the log template has:
- One line per detainee per shift.
- Columns for date/time, key indicators observed, level, action taken, and initials.

For filing, T5 proposes a daily routine where admin staff collect completed A3 forms and update or file A4 in a central folder, with a simple index sheet.

I would like feedback on:
1) Whether the escalation steps and responsibilities in A5 are clear and realistic.
2) Whether the A4 format and the filing routine in T5 are workable on the unit.

@504576 and @297089, your views on the steps and responsibilities would be very helpful. @6456, please check that the wording stays consistent with A2 and A3. I will also prepare a short compliance memo for T11 once we are close to final.

On A5, the overall flow makes sense and matches how we usually handle incidents, with clearer wording.

A few practical comments:
- For Level 2, it says supervisor and medical review. In practice, we often inform the supervisor first, who then decides whether to call medical. Maybe we should reflect that sequence.
- For Level 3, we should explicitly mention that we follow the existing emergency code procedures and legal use-of-force rules, so there is no confusion with current correctional procedures.

On A4, one line per detainee per shift is fine, but we need to be careful that it does not become too time-consuming. Maybe we can allow grouping of uneventful shifts, for example a single line saying no concerning signs observed for that shift.

I have checked A5 against A2 and A3.

The three-level scale is consistent, but I suggest we:
- Use the same terms for the levels as in A2 (monitor, supervisor and possible medical review, emergency response).
- Add a short note in A5 that Level 1 still requires recording in A4, even if no escalation happens, so we can see patterns.

For A4, the columns look good. To support health review, it might help to add a column for follow-up date or next check, so that we can see when a detainee should be reviewed again.

From a coordination and documentation perspective, the structure of A5 is clear.

I agree with @504576 that we should explicitly reference existing emergency codes and legal use-of-force rules, to avoid any impression that this SOP replaces them.

On T5 and A4, the daily admin routine you propose is workable if we keep the log concise. I would suggest:
- Admin staff collect A3 forms at the end of each shift.
- They check that detainee ID and date/time are filled in.
- They file A3 by date and unit, and either update A4 or ensure officers have done so.

We should also define who performs the daily spot check on A4 completeness, as mentioned in the project risks.

Thanks for the detailed feedback.

I will adjust A5 so that for Level 2 the sequence is: officer informs supervisor, supervisor decides on medical review, and both steps are recorded in A4.

For Level 3, I will add a clear reference to the existing emergency code procedures and legal use-of-force rules, and state that this SOP sits alongside, not instead of, those procedures.

On A4, I can add guidance that if there are no concerning signs for a detainee during a shift, officers can tick a no concerning signs box rather than writing a long note, to keep it efficient.

I will align the wording in A5 exactly with the terms used in A2 for the three levels and add the note that Level 1 observations must still be recorded in A4.

I will also add a follow-up date column in A4, so that when a supervisor or medical staff recommend a review, we can track it.

For T5, I will update the filing workflow to include this follow-up information in the daily admin routine.

On the daily spot checks for A4, I suggest that the unit supervisor does a quick review at the end of each day, checking that:
- All detainees on the unit have at least one entry or a no concerning signs tick for the shift.
- Any Level 2 or Level 3 entries have a clear action recorded.

That fits with their current responsibilities and should not add too much extra work.

That sounds reasonable and aligns with the risk mitigation we discussed.

We should capture this in T5 and later in the compliance memo for T11, so it is clear who is accountable for the daily check.

With these adjustments, A5 now clearly links the indicators in A2 and the checklist in A3 to the log A4 and the escalation steps.

From a health perspective, the responsibilities are clear: officers observe and record, supervisors decide on escalation for Level 2, and emergency procedures are followed for Level 3.

I have now incorporated all the feedback into A5 and A4 and updated the T5 filing workflow:
- A5: roles and steps clarified, Level 2 sequence adjusted, Level 3 explicitly references existing emergency and legal use-of-force procedures, wording aligned with A2.
- A4: added follow-up date column and a no concerning signs option, plus guidance on one line per detainee per shift.
- T5: daily admin routine defined, with unit supervisor responsible for daily spot checks on A4.

Before we sign off, could you, @504576, confirm that the escalation steps and responsibilities in A5 are workable on the unit?

I have reviewed the updated A5.

The escalation steps are now clear and match our current practice, with the added structure from A2 and A3. The responsibilities for officers, supervisors, admin, and medical are well defined, and the reference to existing emergency procedures is helpful.

I am comfortable using this version of A5 as the standard for the pilot.

On A4 and the filing workflow in T5, the format and routine look workable from a coordination standpoint.

We have:
- A4 as the central log with clear columns and a no concerning signs option.
- Admin collecting A3 forms and ensuring A4 is updated.
- Unit supervisors doing daily spot checks.
- A central folder with an index sheet for filing.

Unless anyone sees a major issue, I suggest we confirm this as the final format and storage routine for A4 so that T5 can be closed.

From the admin side, I agree. The A4 format and the T5 workflow are clear and fit within our current filing practices.

I will document the routine in more detail and include it in the SOP A5 and in the compliance memo for T11.

To wrap up this thread:
- A5 is now our agreed SOP for health risk assessment and escalation, with clear roles and steps aligned with existing correctional procedures.
- A4 is our central log template, with a defined filing and spot-check routine under T5.

Next, I will draft the compliance alignment and risk memo for T11, mapping A5 and A4 to current procedures and listing key risks and mitigations.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and execute the pilot, then consolidate feedback and improvements.

messages.text:
With A5 and A4 agreed, we should now plan the pilot as per T7 and capture it in A6.

Proposal for the pilot:
- Unit: B-wing residential unit plus the intake area (as per our earlier scope).
- Duration: one full rota cycle of 3 weeks.
- Participants: all officers and assistants on B-wing and intake, with at least one supervisor closely involved.

During the pilot, we will use A3 for intake and patrols, A4 for the central log, and follow A5 for escalation. At the end, we will summarise feedback in A7 and adjust forms and materials via T9 and T10.

Questions:
1) Are B-wing and intake the right places to start, or should we consider a different unit?
2) Are there any scheduling constraints we should factor into A6?

@504576, could you comment on the choice of unit and timing? @19315, can you help with scheduling and documenting the pilot plan for T7?

B-wing and intake are a good choice. B-wing has a mix of detainees, including some with higher health needs, but it is not the most complex unit, so it is manageable for a first pilot.

On timing, starting at the beginning of a rota cycle makes sense. We should avoid the week when we have planned maintenance checks, as that already adds extra paperwork.

For participants, we should include at least one officer from each shift as a point of contact for feedback during T8.

I can take the lead on drafting A6 and coordinating T7.

Based on the rota, the next full cycle without major planned disruptions starts on the 1st of next month. We could:
- Run the pilot from the 1st to the 21st.
- Schedule two briefing sessions in the week before, one for day shifts and one for night shifts.

I will check with prison management to confirm that B-wing and intake are acceptable for the pilot and that the dates work for them.

For the briefings and training materials in T6, I can prepare a short handout and a few scenarios showing how A2, A3, A4, and A5 work together in practice.

If we confirm the pilot dates, I will align the training sessions so that everyone on B-wing and intake has had the 2-hour briefing before the start date.

On the forms side, I will prepare enough printed copies of A3 and A4 for the pilot period under T9, and I can also adjust the layout slightly if we get early feedback in the first few days.

Please let me know the final dates and the number of officers and assistants involved so I can estimate how many copies we need.

Thanks. To move towards a decision on the pilot plan in A6, here is a concrete proposal based on what we have discussed:
- Unit: B-wing residential unit and intake.
- Dates: 1st to 21st of next month.
- Participants: all officers and assistants on B-wing and intake, with one officer per shift acting as a feedback contact.
- Preparation: two briefing sessions in the week before, using the training materials from T6.

If there are no strong objections, I suggest we adopt this as the pilot scope and schedule for A6 and T7.
I support this plan. The dates and units are workable, and the preparation time is sufficient as long as the briefings are scheduled around shift patterns.

I have checked with prison management, and they are comfortable with B-wing and intake as the pilot areas and with the proposed dates.

I will document this in A6 and update T7 with the confirmed scope, dates, and participating staff.

Great, then we will treat the plan you described as the agreed pilot setup for A6.

Next, we should clarify how we will collect feedback during T8 and how we will decide which changes from A7 to apply before wider rollout.

For T8, I suggest we:
- Have a short check-in at the end of each week of the pilot with the feedback contacts from each shift.
- Use a simple form where officers and assistants can note what works, what is difficult, and any incidents where the protocol helped or did not help.

At the end of the pilot, we can summarise this into A7, focusing on practical issues like checklist length, clarity of A5, and the workload of A4.

In the weekly check-ins, it would be useful to capture a few specific examples where the indicators in A2 and the checklist in A3 led to an earlier or clearer escalation, as well as any cases where they did not.

That will help us refine the content in T9 and T10, not just the layout.

From the forms perspective, I would like to know during the pilot:
- Whether there is enough space on A3 for notes.
- Whether the font size is readable in low light.
- Whether officers find the layout intuitive.

We can include a few specific questions about these points in the feedback form for T8, so that T9 has clear input for refining the layout.

I can design a simple feedback form for T8 that covers:
- Ease of use of A3 and A4.
- Clarity of A5 steps.
- Impact on workload.
- Examples where the protocol helped or did not help.

At the end of the pilot, I will compile the responses and the weekly check-in notes into A7, highlighting key issues and suggestions.

Once we have A7, we will need to decide which changes to apply before recommending wider rollout in T10 and T12.

I propose we prioritise changes that:
- Improve clarity or safety without adding significant workload.
- Address recurring issues raised by several officers or assistants.
- Are feasible without changing core IT systems.

More substantial changes that require system updates or policy shifts could be listed as longer-term recommendations in T12.

That prioritisation makes sense from the unit perspective.

For example, if officers consistently say that one item on A3 is unclear or rarely used, we should adjust or remove it before rollout. If they say that A4 takes too long to fill in, we might simplify some fields.

Bigger changes, like integrating with digital systems, can wait until after we see how the paper-based version works.

From the health side, I would argue that any change that clearly improves early detection of serious issues should also be prioritised, even if it adds a small amount of extra work, as long as officers agree it is manageable.

We can flag such changes in A7 so that T9 and T10 focus on them first.

When drafting T10 and T12 after the pilot, I will:
- Apply the agreed priority rules to decide which changes from A7 go into the final A3, A4, and A5.
- Document any larger or longer-term suggestions separately in the rollout recommendation in T12.

To make this transparent, I can include a short table in A7 showing which suggestions were accepted now, which are deferred, and why.

To make this concrete, I suggest we agree now that before wider rollout we will definitely apply:
- Any changes that simplify wording or layout of A3 and A4 without losing content.
- Any changes that clarify steps in A5 where officers report confusion.
- Any additions that clearly improve early detection and are considered manageable by officers.

Other suggestions from A7 will be documented in T12 as future improvements.

If everyone is comfortable with this, we can treat it as our rule for which changes from A7 to implement before rollout.
I agree with that rule. It balances practicality with safety and gives officers confidence that their feedback will lead to visible improvements.
I am comfortable with this approach as well. It gives us a clear framework for deciding which changes from A7 go into T9 and T10 before we recommend wider rollout in T12.

I will note this rule in the pilot plan A6 and in the structure of A7, so that when we reach T10 and T12, it is clear how we decided which changes to implement now.

We can then say that the agreed changes from A7 have been applied before recommending rollout.

To summarise this thread:
- Pilot unit and dates are confirmed in A6: B-wing and intake, 1st to 21st of next month, with all officers and assistants participating.
- T7 will cover finalising the plan and scheduling briefings; T8 will run the pilot and collect feedback using forms and weekly check-ins.
- A7 will summarise feedback, and we have agreed a rule for which changes to apply before rollout: those that simplify wording or layout, clarify steps, or clearly improve early detection while remaining manageable.

These agreed changes from A7 will be implemented through T9 and T10 before we prepare the final rollout recommendation in T12.
